chapters.title: Chapter 21 · Two Years of Quiet Work
chapters.artPrompt: a red-haired girl reading under a big maple tree beside a farmhouse porch, books and a notebook in the grass, soft summer afternoon light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: So the two years passed, quietly and quickly, the way happy, busy years do. In spring there were armfuls of violets in Violet Vale, brought home to Marilla in triumph. In summer the grammar was carried out to the orchard and conjugated among the bees. In autumn there were long drives under red maples. In winter there were lamp-lit evenings, with the wind singing in the eaves. It was, Anne said later, the fullest two years a girl ever spent.
Anne studies in the orchard among the bees.

Anne grew taller, and quieter, though nobody who knew her would truly call her quiet. Her braids grew longer; so did her sentences. She still tumbled into scrapes, but fewer, and she climbed out of them more gracefully. Marilla said she was learning sense. Anne said she was only learning which of her mistakes would make the best stories. Diana heard every detail of everything, and could conjugate nothing, and knew it all anyway. It was a good arrangement, and it lasted.
New word: grammar — the rules by which words fit together. Anne and grammar ended their long war with honour on both sides.

Matthew walked slower on the lane now, and took longer rests by the gate. Nobody worried; that was just Matthew. He asked about the lessons at supper every night. He listened as if the answers were news from a far country. The light in the east gable burned on. The lists grew shorter, and the examination drew near.

At last it was summer again — the examination summer. Miss Stacy held a final trial of all they knew, and Anne came through with colours flying. One August morning the candidates would take the train for Charlottetown. Anne laid out her second-best dress and could not eat her supper. Marilla starched her collar without being asked, which meant more than speeches. Tomorrow, the first true door of her life would stand open. She meant to walk through it with her head up.

chapters.title: Chapter 22 · The Day of the Exam
chapters.artPrompt: rows of students writing at desks in a grand examination hall, a red-haired girl bent over her paper, tall windows and dust motes in slanting light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: On a bright August morning, the Queen's candidates of Avonlea took the train to Charlottetown. The town was big and busy, all hurry and shine. Anne looked at the shop windows with her eyes, but her mind was elsewhere. Somewhere in the crowd she bought a pencil she did not need, just to have something to hold. In a great hall, rows of desks stood waiting, each with a name card upon it.
Anne writes her entrance examination in the big hall.

For three days they wrote: composition and history, sums and grammar, geography and everything. The hall clock ticked like a walking stick on stone. Question after question marched past like soldiers, and Anne answered them as fast as they came. When she came out at noon she could not remember what she had written. Diana had once told her that was a good sign. Gilbert came out frowning one day and whistling the next, and everyone knew the examination was seeing to its favourites.
New word: candidate — a person competing for a place or a prize. Anne was a candidate for Queen's, and ate very little all week.

Then it was over, and there was nothing to do but wait. The lists would be printed in the newspaper when the examiners had finished. Anne went home and tried to be useful, and was a great deal in the way. She weeded the garden, and read, and walked to the gate a hundred times a day. She was watching for the postman. Matthew said the corn never grew faster than it grew that week, Anne walked the lane so much.

She was afraid, of course. Afraid of failing, and of failing in front of Gilbert Blythe. Afraid of disappointing Miss Stacy, and the quiet faces at Green Gables. But at night, in the east gable, she made herself say what Miss Stacy had taught her. Whatever comes, I have done my honest best — and tomorrow is always fresh, with no mistakes in it yet. It did not stop the waiting. But it made the waiting bearable.

chapters.title: Chapter 23 · The Pass List Is Out
chapters.artPrompt: a grey-haired farm couple and a red-haired girl around a kitchen table reading a newspaper, the girl's hands clasped, warm evening lamplight, storybook illustration

blocks.text: At last the paper came. It was dinnertime when the news arrived. Marilla took the newspaper. Matthew stopped eating. Anne stood very straight in the middle of the kitchen, not daring to sit. Anne's hands were cold as snow. The kitchen clock ticked four times before anybody spoke. Marilla read the pass list slowly. And at the top of the list — at the very top — stood the name of Anne Shirley.
Marilla reads the pass list while Matthew and Anne hold their breath.

Gilbert Blythe's name stood beside it. Both had passed, at the head of all the candidates on the Island. Anne sat down at last, and laughed, and nearly cried, and did both a little. Matthew came around the table. “I'd rather have you than a dozen boys,” he said — which, for Matthew, was a speech of an hour. Then he went out to the barn, because his eyes needed attending to. Marilla said the fresh bread was burning, though it was not, because hers did too.
New word: pass — to succeed in an examination. To fail is its opposite, and no one at Green Gables failed that day.

The news ran down the lane faster than Anne could. By evening Mrs. Rachel Lynde had arrived to say she had always known it. “First of all!” she told three neighbours before supper. Mrs. Allan sent a kind note. Even Josie Pye said “Congratulations” in a voice with a small splinter in it. Diana hugged Anne on the doorstep and danced her round, and said it was almost as good as passing herself.

There was one more door ahead: Queen's itself, in Charlottetown, beginning in September. But first there would be the whole of August. There would be haying, and picnics, and one grand evening Anne did not know was coming. That night she wrote to Miss Stacy. “I passed at the top, and I could not have done it without you,” she wrote. It was the plainest true thing she knew how to say.

chapters.title: Chapter 24 · The Dress for White Sands
chapters.artPrompt: a red-haired girl and her dark-haired friend preparing a best dress in a lamplit bedroom, ribbons and a hairbrush on the table, soft evening light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The surprise came in August. The ladies of Avonlea were arranging a charity concert at the White Sands Hotel. It was the big house by the sea where the summer visitors stayed. The best performers for miles were asked to take part, and a famous reciter from town was to come. And Anne was asked to recite. She read the invitation three times. She said yes with her voice, and nearly fainted with the rest of her.
Anne and Diana prepare for the great evening at White Sands.

For two weeks the whole house revolved around it. Anne practiced morning and night: to the mirror, to the cows, and to an audience of dishes. Diana came every evening to listen and clap. The question of the dress was almost as serious as the recitation. Everything Anne owned was tried on twice, and the mirror was consulted like an oracle. “It is the biggest thing I have ever done,” Anne told her reflection, “and you are not helping.” Marilla pretended not to care, and cared completely.
New word: charity — help given to people who need it. The concert would raise money for a good work.

The great evening came at last. At sunset Matthew drove Anne and Diana to White Sands in the buggy. The hotel sat above the water like a crown of lamps. Inside, the long hall glittered with strangers — summer visitors in silk, and farmers' families in their best. Anne stood at the door and felt her courage slip away like water. Somewhere in the hall, she knew, was at least one person who wished her well.

Diana pressed her hand. “Remember,” she said, “you have recited to cows all month. This is only a larger field.” Anne laughed — a real laugh — and her shoulders came down. A singer sang, and the hall roared its pleasure. The famous reciter recited, and the hall held its breath. Then a name was called. A red-haired girl walked out alone onto the great platform, and the lamps were suddenly very bright.

chapters.title: Chapter 25 · The Hotel Concert
chapters.artPrompt: a red-haired girl in a white dress reciting on a grand hotel stage before a glittering audience, chandeliers and silk gowns, golden lamplight by the sea, storybook illustration

blocks.text: For one breath Anne could not remember a single word. The hall was a wall of faces, and her hands, in their white gloves, were ice at the fingertips. Then she heard her own voice begin, clear and steady, as if from a little distance. The poem rose like a bird. The stillness after her first lines told her the whole hall was listening. Something in Anne, the something that was more than shyness, took wing.
Anne recites at the great concert at White Sands Hotel.

She gave them laughter, and she gave them tears. When the last line fell, the applause came like surf, and they called her back — once, twice. The ladies in silk nodded at one another: who was that girl? The famous reciter from town shook her hand afterward, and told her the poem had never sounded so fresh. Anne carried those words out to the buggy like a lantern.
New word: encore — a call from the audience for a performer to come back again. Anne had one, and glowed for a week.

The drive home was all stars and slow wheels. Matthew drove, and said little, and meant all of it. The sea sighed against the cliffs below the road. Diana slept on Anne's shoulder before they were halfway home. Anne watched the stars the whole way, too happy to blink. “I wish Green Gables could have seen it,” she whispered to the sleeping world. Then she remembered that Green Gables, in the person of Matthew, had.
Talk together: When have you been frightened to do something, and then done it well?

At Green Gables she lay awake a long time, counting every moment like beads. The girl whom nobody had wanted had stood on a platform by the sea. Strangers had called her back twice. Tomorrow it would be a memory; but the courage was hers to keep. In September she would take the train to Queen's. This night would go with her, packed where she could find it. It was proof, whenever she doubted, that fear could be walked through.

chapters.title: Chapter 26 · Goodbye to Green Gables
chapters.artPrompt: an elderly man and a red-haired girl beside a packed trunk at a small railway platform, a grey-haired woman in a bonnet waving from a buggy, soft morning light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: September came, and the trunk stood packed in the hall. Into it went the brown dress with puffed sleeves, and the plain best dresses. There was the grammar, and a little bag of things too precious to name. Anne looked around her room at the low ceiling and the east window. She could not quite believe she was leaving it. Marilla folded and refolded things that were already flat.
Matthew and Anne wait with the trunk at Bright River station.

Matthew drove her to Bright River station, where he had found her five years before. Marilla came to the gate. Goodbye was said briskly, because Marilla could not say it any other way. Then, just as Anne climbed up, Marilla reached up too, and kissed her — once, quickly, on the cheek. She turned back to the house at once, as if there were urgent business inside. Anne sat very still for the first mile. She had waited five years for that kiss.
New word: trunk — a big box for clothes, used for travelling. Anne's trunk held most of what she owned in the world.

The train ran through the autumn country, past farms she knew and farms she did not. Anne watched until the maples of home dropped below a hill. Then she gave her eyes to the future: Queen's, and work, and a prize to win. Her head was full of plans. A boy with a violin case got in at one stop, and life felt suddenly wide. But her heart, for a while, ran back along the rails behind her.

“Work hard,” Matthew had said at the window, “and don't fret about home. Home will keep.” Anne held those words all the way to town. It was the longest speech Matthew had ever made her, and the kindest. Somewhere behind her, Green Gables sat under its hill of maples, keeping, as promised. And somewhere ahead waited the city, and Queen's, and the busy, brilliant year that would change everything. It would not change things only in the ways she imagined.

chapters.title: Chapter 27 · First Days at Queen's
chapters.artPrompt: a red-haired girl with books under her arm gazing up at a tall brick academy building on a busy town street, autumn leaves and omnibuses, bright morning light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Charlottetown swallowed Anne whole — kindly, but whole. There were omnibuses and pavements and shopfronts, glass and noise and fashion. Anne walked into it all with her nose lifted, like a kitten at a fair. Queen's Academy was full of strangers who all seemed to know exactly where to go. Anne and some of the other country girls had rooms together near the Academy. Her window looked out on other people's roofs, which was, she decided, interesting in its way.
Anne arrives at Queen's Academy in the busy town.

The work began at once, and it was enormous. There were professors instead of one Miss Stacy. Each seemed to think his own subject the only one in the world. Anne took notes until her hand ached, and walked home in a dream of dates and theorems. In the next room lived Priscilla Grant, calm and smiling, who became Anne's first new friend. Priscilla never worried about anything, which fascinated Anne like a foreign language. Gilbert Blythe was there too, and other Avonlea faces, and it was a comfort — even at a distance.
New word: professor — a teacher at a college or academy. Professors assign reading the way rain assigns puddles.

At night came the homesickness. It came quietly, around lamplight, when the roofs outside went dark. Anne missed the sound of the wind in the big kitchen chimney. She missed the Barry pond, Matthew's chair, and Marilla's step on the stair. She wrote a long letter home and posted it before she could be sensible about it. Letters went both ways all that year, and every one of them smelled, to Anne, faintly of Green Gables.

By October the city was not a giant anymore, only a busy neighbour. Anne knew the short cuts and the smell of the different streets. She was small no longer in her own eyes. Queen's had already taught her one lesson no class could teach. A girl who could survive her first week in a strange city could survive a great deal more.

chapters.title: Chapter 28 · The Winter at Queen's
chapters.artPrompt: a red-haired girl studying at a small desk by a boarding-house window while snow falls past the glass, warm lamplight, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Winter came down on Charlottetown, and Queen's warmed itself with work. The two-year course lay ahead of every student. But near Christmas, Anne made a resolve that made her landlady put down her teapot. She would do the two years of work in one. Then, next autumn, she could go on to Redmond College. It meant giving up part of the spring vacation and every idle evening. The landlady said scholars were her favourite lodgers. Anne signed away her evenings without one regret.
Anne studies through the snowy winter at Queen's.

The winter that followed was the busiest and, in its fierce way, the happiest of her life. Days were lectures; evenings were the lamp; Sundays were letters home. Anne grew pale and thin and entirely alive. Sometimes she and Priscilla made cocoa and talked until the fire fell in. The kettle was always warm. The girls in the house adopted her. By February, Anne could not remember being afraid of anything so small as a city.
Talk together: Anne missed home but made herself at home. What helps you feel at home in a new place?

At midwinter the marks went up, and the race was on again. Anne Shirley and Gilbert Blythe traded first place like two skaters passing each other on a pond. One month the list said Gilbert; the next it said Anne. They never spoke of it, which made it worse — or better. Anne worked hardest exactly when he was ahead. In honest moments, she suspected that he did the same because of her. Priscilla said the list should simply print both names and be done.

Letters flew home, and parcels flew back with cake in them. Spring arrived in the town before anyone was ready. The two-years-in-one students bent over their books like swimmers in the last length. Everything Anne had was in the race now. Every Violet Vale evening, every lamp-lit list, all of it swimming toward June. The race did not pause for anybody.

chapters.title: Chapter 29 · Two Years in One
chapters.artPrompt: a tired but determined red-haired girl writing an examination paper in a crowded hall, a clock on the wall, pale summer light through high windows, storybook illustration

blocks.text: June came, and with it the final examinations — twice as long as any Anne had sat before. For two years of work in one year, she had to answer for both. The hall was hot, and the pens scratched. Anne wrote until her wrist ached and her eyes swam. She went home each evening too tired to be frightened, which was perhaps the plan.
Anne writes the great final examinations at Queen's.

At last it was done. Anne walked out of Queen's feeling as tall as a church, and as empty as one. The other students scattered for the summer, chattering about dances and the shore. The results would be read at the closing ceremony, on the platform, before everyone. There was nothing left to study, and it was the strangest feeling of her life. She and the others walked the streets for hours, too restless for rooms. Gilbert looked as calm as ever, which Anne found comforting and infuriating in equal part.
New word: ceremony — a formal gathering with speeches and prizes. Queen's would end its year with one.

Home for a week, Anne helped Marilla with the early peas. She hung over the gate with Diana, and was no use to anybody. Matthew asked twice a day if there was news. Marilla pretended the whole business was neither here nor there, and polished the good spoons for no reason. Even the hens seemed to wait. Diana said waiting was worse than examinations. Anne said waiting was worse than anything ever invented.

At night Anne lay awake and reviewed, not her lessons, but her luck. Born a nobody, and given Green Gables. Given Matthew and Marilla, Diana and Miss Stacy. Whatever the lists said, she had already been paid a thousand times over. But she wanted the prize still — honestly, hungrily. The Avery scholarship would pay her way through Redmond College; without it, Redmond was only a beautiful word. “If I win it, it will be theirs as much as mine,” she thought. “Every violet of it.”

chapters.title: Chapter 30 · The Avery Scholarship
chapters.artPrompt: a red-haired girl in a white dress receiving a paper scroll on a stage hung with flags, a hall of students and families applauding, bright ceremonial light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Queen's closed its year with flags and speeches and a hall full of families. The hall smelled of flowers. Matthew and Marilla had not come; it was haying time. So Anne sat with her class, her hands folded, her heart hammering. Prizes were called out one by one: books and certificates, to the steady applause of parents. Everyone knew the two great prizes of the year were the twin summits of everything.
Anne receives the Avery scholarship at the closing ceremony.

Then the big prizes were called. The gold medal of the year — and the name was Gilbert Blythe. Gilbert went up through applause to receive it, steady and smiling. Anne clapped until her hands hurt. The hall waited. Her turn, said her hammering heart; and her turn might not come; and both were suddenly, equally possible.
New word: scholarship — money awarded to a student to pay for further study. The Avery was the greatest one.

And then: “The Avery scholarship, to be held at Redmond College, is awarded to — Anne Shirley.” The hall's noise reached her as if through water. Anne walked the long floor on shaking legs, and the paper in her hand weighed nothing and everything. Her year's whole long race had just crossed its finish line. Gilbert's medal and her scholarship, honours even at the last, the way the story had always gone.

Her first clear thought was that Matthew should have heard it. Her second was to find Priscilla, who was crying and applauding at once, which is a difficult trick. That evening the Avonlea students took the train home through the late gold light. The summer, wide and green, received them. Marilla read the prize letter aloud twice. Anne carried the scholarship home like a candle in a jar: light for later, and warmth for now. In September, Redmond. But first, one whole summer at Green Gables. She did not know — nobody knew — what that summer would ask of her.

chapters.title: Chapter 31 · Summer at Green Gables
chapters.artPrompt: a red-haired girl and an elderly man standing at a farm gate looking over golden hayfields at dusk, quiet warm light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: It was the greenest summer Anne could remember. She was home with the prize won, and the whole golden holiday before her. Redmond waited in September, like a door standing open. She read in the orchard and walked the lanes with Diana, and told Marilla everything twice. The raspberries were heavy that year; even the hens seemed prosperous. But Marilla looked smaller in the kitchen doorway than she used to. Her hair had gone grey at the front. Anne noticed, and filed the noticing away, and kept on being happy.
Anne and Matthew stand at the gate over the golden fields.

Matthew was proud of her that summer, in Matthew's way. He said nothing to Anne, and everything at the store. Anne heard from three neighbours that Matthew Cuthbert's girl had won the biggest prize on the Island. She teased him about it at the gate one evening. He went red, and smiled at his boots. The evenings were long and mild, and the smell of the hayfields came up to the porch. Anne thought: this is the best year of my life.
Talk together: Anne counted her blessings that summer. What are three of yours?

There were plans, too. Redmond in the autumn, and college beyond, and after that — Anne spread her hands — everything. She would study, and write, and see the world, and come back wiser to Green Gables between times. It never once occurred to her that the world might not wait. It never once occurred to her that plans are written in pencil.

In late August the first evening came that felt like autumn. Anne stood at the east window and smelled the change. The maples were still green, but the light had a thin gold edge on it now. Below her, Matthew stood by the gate looking at his fields, leaning on the bars as he always had. She waved, and he lifted his hand. The summer, like the lane, bent toward autumn. Anne went to bed that night with a heart as light as a leaf.

chapters.title: Chapter 32 · The Bank Fails
chapters.artPrompt: an elderly farmer sitting at a kitchen table staring at a newspaper, a red-haired girl and a grey-haired woman watching him with fear, dim evening light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The news came by newspaper, as bad news often does. It was an ordinary Tuesday. Anne was darning socks when the buggy drove in. One evening the Charlottetown paper came with the mail. In it was a short notice: the Abbey Bank had failed. All the Cuthbert savings — years and years of farm money — lay in that bank. Matthew read the notice at the table. He read it twice. “If that is true,” he said, in a strange small voice, “it will mean —” He never finished the sentence. Marilla gently took the paper from him.
Matthew reads the terrible news about the bank.

He had trusted that bank as he trusted rain. Marilla said little; there was nothing to say that would help. That same evening, crossing the yard at sunset, Matthew fell, and his heart stopped as gently as he had lived. The doctor, when he came, could only say the heart had been tired for years. There had been no pain.
New word: fail — when a bank fails, it closes its doors and the money in it may be lost. The Cuthberts had trusted one bank all their lives.

It could not be. But it was. All that night and all the next day, Anne moved through the house like a girl underwater. The kitchen fire spoke softly to itself. Matthew, who had brought her home from Bright River station. Matthew, who said nothing and did everything. Matthew, who thought she was worth a dozen boys, whose love had never once needed words. Gone between the barn and the door, between one ordinary evening and the next.

The church was full for the funeral. Farmers came from far away, and even strangers spoke of his quiet kindness. “He was a good man,” they said, “the steadiest man on the road.” Over and over, kindly, until the words wore smooth. Anne sat beside Marilla and did not cry. She could not. The tears would not come, and their not coming frightened her more than anything.

chapters.title: Chapter 33 · The Days After
chapters.artPrompt: a red-haired girl resting her head against an open window frame at sunset, tears on her face, a quiet farmyard and dark maples beyond, amber light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: For a week after the funeral Anne did not cry at all. The house was very quiet; even the clock seemed to walk on tiptoe. Marilla washed, and ironed, and cooked, because work was her way of standing upright. Anne studied her own hands as if they belonged to somebody else. The sunshine went on and on, and Anne was almost angry at the sun for shining. The hens looked thinner. The lane looked longer. Everything looked like Matthew. Diana wept for her, it seemed, since Anne could not.
Anne finds the first soft comfort at her east window.

Then one evening, at the east window, the sun went down behind the maples. It fell in a great slow splendour of rose and amber. Something in Anne broke open — no, opened. The world was still beautiful; Matthew had loved this very view. And grief, all at once, had a door in it. She said his name out loud, once, softly. She cried at last, quietly, for a long time, with the window open. Somewhere in it she felt, or believed she felt, Matthew's kindness in the room. It was enough.
New word: funeral — the ceremony at which friends say goodbye to someone who has died.
Talk together: Who helped Anne most in the sad days? Who would help you?

That night Marilla, who never wept, wept at the kitchen table, and Anne held her as long as she needed. “We have each other,” said Anne at last. “That is not nothing.” The neighbours were endless, with dishes of food and gentle errands. Diana came every single day, sometimes with words and sometimes only with her presence, which was worth more. She brought forget-me-nots from her own garden every week. Mrs. Allan came and said the true thing. Grief, she said, is love with nowhere to go. It must find new places to go to. It helped more than anything. Slowly the house learned its new shape. Matthew's chair was still by the window. Nobody moved it, and that was right.

chapters.title: Chapter 34 · Marilla's Eyes
chapters.artPrompt: a stern kind-faced grey-haired woman and a red-haired girl walking slowly from a town doctor's door, the girl holding the woman's arm, soft overcast light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Marilla had complained, for her, a great deal about her eyes all autumn. Letters swam; needles blurred. “It is nothing,” said Marilla, which was what she always said about anything that was something. So the doctor in town sent her to an oculist, an eye doctor, in the city. Anne went with her. Nothing that Anne imagined on the train was as heavy as the verdict.
Anne walks home with Marilla after the eye doctor's verdict.

The oculist was blunt. If Marilla gave up all reading and all fine sewing, forever, her eyes could be saved. They would serve her for useful work. If not, she would lose her sight altogether, and soon. The word blindness hung in the little room like smoke. Marilla took it standing. On the street afterward she was silent for a whole block. Then she said, with a dry little laugh, that she supposed she had read enough books for one lifetime. Anne heard what the laugh was covering, and could not speak.
New word: oculist — an eye doctor. Marilla was to rest her eyes completely, and hope.

And that was not all. With no reading, no sewing, and careful days, Marilla could not run Green Gables alone. A hired man must be fed and paid, and the bank had taken so much already. “I suppose,” said Marilla, in the kitchen that night, “we shall have to sell Green Gables.” She said it steadily, looking at the table. It was the worst thing Anne had ever heard her say.

“No.” Anne said it out loud, before she had planned to. “We will not sell Green Gables. Selling it would break Matthew's heart still. There is always a way, when a thing means enough.” That night, in the east gable, she took out her plans for Redmond. She looked at them a long time, like a letter from someone she used to be. Then she folded them away. She was not crying. Something in her had already, quietly, decided.

chapters.title: Chapter 35 · Anne's Choice
chapters.artPrompt: a red-haired girl and a grey-haired woman talking earnestly across a lamplit farmhouse kitchen table, warm evening light and tea, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Anne announced it at breakfast the next morning, plainly, the way Marilla herself would have. She was not going to Redmond. She would stay at Green Gables, teach school, and be Marilla's eyes and hands. “I can learn as much here as in any city,” said Anne, “and be of use besides.” Marilla's protest came fast and hot. It was nonsense; the prize was won; she would not hear of it. Anne waited it out like weather.
Anne tells Marilla her decision at the kitchen table.

“You gave me a home when I was eleven and nobody's,” said Anne. “Do you think I would leave you now? Redmond can wait. There are other years; there is only one Green Gables, and only one of you.” Marilla turned to the stove and was extremely busy with it. “You are a foolish, good child,” she said at last, in a voice that was not quite steady. That was the end of the argument.
Talk together: Anne gave up her dream to care for Marilla. What do you think of her choice?

The pieces fell together quickly after that. Mrs. Rachel Lynde knew everything within a day. She arrived to say she would come and keep house at Green Gables. Then the farm could be kept and run. The kitchen rang with plans: the hens, the fall planting, the garden. Marilla and she would grow old together, Anne decided, like two friendly apple trees in one orchard.

One question remained: which school would Anne teach? The little Avonlea school, a mile from her own door, was the one she wanted — of course it was. That evening Anne wrote to Diana: “I am to be an Avonlea girl still. I find, to my astonishment, that I am glad — gladder than I know how to say. The bend in my road has turned, and it turns toward home.” It was true. Somewhere under the loss of that year, something in Anne was settling, like a bird coming down to roost.

chapters.title: Chapter 36 · A Rival's Kindness
chapters.artPrompt: a red-haired girl standing very still in a farm kitchen while a plump kindly older neighbour tells her startling news, firelight and evening, storybook illustration

blocks.text: Then came the second piece of news, and it undid Anne completely. The Avonlea trustees had already given the school — to Gilbert Blythe. Anne heard it first, and her heart went down like a stone. Some other school, then, perhaps far away. But before a day was out, Mrs. Lynde arrived with the rest of it. When Gilbert heard of Green Gables' trouble, he had gone to the trustees and resigned Avonlea on the spot. He would teach at White Sands instead, a school farther from his own home. So the Avonlea school might be Anne's.
Mrs. Lynde tells Anne what Gilbert has done for her.

Anne sat down without meaning to. Five years of keeping her grudge polished like a stove. And all that time, he had been thinking kindly of her. All the slate-cracking, she saw now, had been half her own doing. “It is a terrible thing,” she said slowly, “to be outdone in generosity by someone you have been unjust to.” She stood very still in the middle of the kitchen, with the fire ticking. She rewrote five years of her own opinion in about four seconds.
New word: trustees — the local people who look after a village school and choose its teacher.

“I shall thank him,” Anne said. She put on her hat at once, which showed how serious she was, for Anne and impulse were old friends. Then she took it off again, because it was nearly dark. Tomorrow. One should meet a great kindness in daylight, with one's hair properly braided. Diana, hearing it, said “At last!” in a way that covered five years of patience. Some things should not be hurried, and a first sincere thank-you was one of them.

She told Marilla at supper. Marilla was silent a moment. “Well,” she said, “that was well done.” It was the highest mark Marilla gave, and Anne knew it. Upstairs, Anne looked at herself in the small glass and confessed the whole truth at last. She had never really hated Gilbert Blythe. She had only been proud. And tomorrow, she meant to stop. It felt strangely like the first day of something.

chapters.title: Chapter 37 · Friends at Last
chapters.artPrompt: a red-haired girl and a brown-haired young man talking and laughing on a leaf-strewn lane at dusk, a farmhouse gate behind them, warm low light, storybook illustration

blocks.text: The chance came the very next evening. Anne was out walking her thank-you, as she privately called it, when Gilbert Blythe himself came swinging along the road. The evening was mild, with a smell of cut hay and the first red leaves. He might have lifted his cap and gone by. Instead, seeing her face, he stopped.
Anne and Gilbert talk at last on the Avonlea lane.

“Gilbert,” said Anne, before her courage could escape, “I want to thank you. About the school. Mrs. Lynde told me.” There was a small silence, in which five years quietly died. “It was nothing,” said Gilbert. “Avonlea needs you more. I know what Green Gables means.” He said it simply, without a syllable of sacrifice in it, which made it twice as fine. Then they were walking down the long lane together, without either of them arranging it. They talked of schools and pupils as easily as if they had done it for years.
Talk together: It took Anne five years to forgive one small tease. Why is forgiving so hard — and so freeing?

Somewhere past the orchard they came, by degrees, to the old subject. “I have owed you an apology since the day of the slate,” said Anne. Gilbert laughed until the lane rang. “We were children,” he said. “Carrots!” And at that word, which had once been an insult, they both laughed until the maples shook. The word that had once been war became, in one evening, a joke. That is what most wars are, seen from far enough off.

At the gate of Green Gables they stopped. “Friends,” said Gilbert, holding out his hand. “Real ones.” Anne put her hand in it. “Real ones,” she said. Gilbert went away down the dusk toward White Sands. Anne ran up the lane and burst into the kitchen like weather. Marilla took one look. “Well?” said Marilla. “Gilbert and I are friends,” said Anne. “Properly. Finally.” “It is early days to look so pleased about it,” said Marilla. But she was smiling at the teapot. That night Anne fell asleep counting, not sheep, but kindnesses — and Gilbert's was the tallest of them all.

chapters.title: Chapter 38 · The Bend in the Road
chapters.artPrompt: a red-haired girl leaning at an open gable window at night looking toward a country road that bends into dusk beyond dark maples, a lamp glowing behind her, storybook illustration

blocks.text: A few evenings later, Anne stood at the east gable window. The crickets were stitching the dark together, stitch by stitch. Below her the garden lay dim. Beyond it the lane ran down to the road, and the road bent away into the dusk. She had stood at this window on her first night at Green Gables. She had been an unwanted orphan, afraid of being sent back. So much road since then.
Anne watches the road bend into the dusk from her window.

“When I left Queen's, my road seemed to run straight,” she told the window. “Redmond, and glory, and everything planned. Now there is a bend in it, and I cannot see past the bend. But that is the excitement of a road, is it not — the bending? I mean to believe that the best lies around it. Nothing has gone as planned, and everything, somehow, has gone right.” There would be the little school and its noise. There would be Green Gables under snow, and spring coming up the lane every year, faithful as a friend.
Talk together: What do you hope lies around your bend in the road?

Downstairs, Marilla sat by the lamp with her eyes resting, as the doctor had ordered, on nothing at all. She called up to ask if Anne was asleep. “No,” Anne called back. “Only thinking.” “Think kindly of the world,” said Marilla. “It has used us well enough.” From Marilla, it was a long speech, and Anne treasured it.

Far off toward White Sands, a lamp or two glimmered. A young schoolmaster there was preparing lessons. It was too far to see, but Anne smiled at it anyway. Tomorrow she would clean the little schoolhouse; on Monday she would meet her first class. Miss Stacy's old words came back to her, as they did at every beginning. Tomorrow is always fresh, with no mistakes in it yet. The road bent, the night gathered, and the maples stood dark and patient. Anne leaned her cheek against the cool glass. “God's in his heaven,” she whispered, “all's right with the world.” And with her — with the whole winding, shining road of it — it was.
